hints: Picture the six carbon atoms of benzene in space and recall what regular shape lets all C-C bond angles be equal and as wide as possible.
Think about how many sigma bonded regions each carbon has in benzene and what hybridisation that implies for trigonal geometry.
Consider which unhybridised orbital is left over on each carbon after hybridisation and how it is oriented relative to the ring plane.
Compare end on overlap along the bond axis with sideways overlap above and below the plane to decide which gives sigma and which gives pi bonding.
walkthrough:
See the flat hexagon**
Imagine six carbons joined in a ring. They all lie in exactly the same plane, forming a perfect regular hexagon. That flat shape keeps every C-C-C angle at $120^{\circ}$, which is the ideal angle for three groups arranged trigonally around each carbon with minimum repulsion.

Link shape to sp2 hybridisation**
Each carbon in benzene bonds to two other carbons and one hydrogen by sigma bonds, so three sigma regions in total. That is classic trigonal planar electron geometry, made by promoting and mixing one 2s with two 2p orbitals to give three $\text{sp}^2$ hybrid orbitals at $120^{\circ}$, leaving one unhybridised p orbital per carbon.

Build the sigma framework**
The $\text{sp}^2$ orbitals point directly at neighbours in the plane of the ring. When two $\text{sp}^2$ orbitals meet head on along the C-C axis they overlap end on to make a strong $\sigma$ bond. The same type of end on overlap makes the C-H $\sigma$ bonds.

Add the pi system above and below**
The leftover p orbital on each carbon sticks up and down perpendicular to the ring plane. Neighbouring p orbitals overlap sideways, not head on, above and below the ring. In benzene all six p orbitals merge into one delocalised $\pi$ system with electron density in two doughnut shaped clouds above and below the planar sigma framework.

Final answer: Benzene ring is planar hexagonal, trigonal planar around each C, bond angle $120^{\circ}$. Each C is $\text{sp}^2$ hybridised. $\text{sp}^2$ orbitals overlap end on to form $\sigma$ bonds between C atoms. Unused p orbitals overlap sideways above and below the ring to form $\pi$ bonds, giving a delocalised $\pi$ system.

hints: For reaction 5, compare the reactant and product rings and decide what has happened to the delocalised pi system and what reagent adds hydrogen across it.
For reaction 6, look at the new $\text{-COCH(CH}_3)_2$ group on the ring and recall which acyl compound plus Lewis acid catalyst installs an acyl group.
walkthrough:
Read reaction 5 as loss of aromaticity**
Benzoic acid with its aromatic ring becomes cyclohexanecarboxylic acid with a fully saturated ring. You have added three molecules of $\text{H}_2$ across the three pi bonds. Benzene is very stable, so this needs vigorous catalytic hydrogenation with $\text{H}_2$ passed over heated $\text{Pt}$ or $\text{Ni}$ catalyst.

Read reaction 6 as acylation**
The product keeps the benzene ring but gains a $\text{-COCH(CH}_3)_2$ ketone side chain. That is Friedel-Crafts acylation, electrophilic substitution by an acylium ion. Use the acyl chloride $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOCl}$ plus the Lewis acid catalyst $\text{AlCl}_3$ with heating to generate the electrophile.

Final answer: reaction 5: $\text{H}_2$ with $\text{Pt}$ or $\text{Ni}$ catalyst, with heat.
reaction 6: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOCl}$ with $\text{AlCl}_3$ catalyst, with heat.

hints: Focus on the change in hydrogen to carbon ratio when the aromatic ring becomes a saturated cyclohexane ring.
walkthrough:
Classify by hydrogen gain**
Going from $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$ to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}$ is a gain of hydrogen, which is reduction. Because $\text{H}_2$ is added across multiple bonds with a metal catalyst, the specific name is hydrogenation, a type of reduction.

hints: Recall whether alkyl groups push electrons toward the ring or pull them away, and which ring positions that activates.
walkthrough:
Place alkyl groups in the directing family**
Alkyl groups like $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ push electron density toward the ring by the positive inductive effect. That makes the ring more reactive and stabilises the intermediate best when the electrophile attacks ortho (2, 6) or para (4) to the alkyl group, so they are 2,4-directors.
Final answer: $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ is 2,4-directing (ortho, para directing) because it is an electron donating group.

hints: Think of $\text{FeBr}_3$ as a bromide ion acceptor that pulls $\text{Br}^-$ from $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ to leave a carbocation.
walkthrough:
Let the Lewis acid create the electrophile**
$\text{FeBr}_3$ is electron deficient and accepts $\text{Br}^-$ from bromoethane. The C-Br bond breaks heterolytically, giving the ethyl carbocation electrophile $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^+$ and the tetrabromoferrate ion $\text{FeBr}_4^-$. Keep charges and atoms balanced: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{FeBr}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^+ + \text{FeBr}_4^-$$

hints: Start from the delocalised pi electrons of the benzene ring attacking the positively charged carbon of $\text{^+CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
Draw the positively charged cyclohexadienyl cation intermediate with the new C-C bond and the disrupted aromaticity.
Consider how the C-H bond at the substituted carbon breaks to restore the aromatic ring and what small ion is expelled.
walkthrough:
Attack of the ring on the electrophile**
The benzene pi cloud is electron rich and the $\text{^+CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ carbon is electron poor. Draw a curly arrow starting inside the hexagon, representing the pi electrons, and pointing to the $\text{C}^+$ of the ethyl cation to make a new C-C bond. Aromaticity is temporarily lost.

Draw the Wheland intermediate**
You now have a cyclohexadienyl cation, often called the arenium ion or sigma complex. The ring has the $\text{-COOH}$ group still attached, plus the new $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ group, one carbon is $\text{sp}^3$ with an extra H, and the positive charge is delocalised over the remaining five carbons. Show the + charge on the ring.

Restore aromaticity by losing H+**
Draw a curly arrow from the C-H bond on the $\text{sp}^3$ carbon back into the ring. That pair of electrons reforms the pi system and ejects $\text{H}^+$. The flat aromatic ring returns, giving the para substituted product shown in Fig. 5.2 plus $\text{H}^+$.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene $\pi$ system to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^+$ to form arenium ion intermediate with $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ attached and positive charge delocalised in ring. Curly arrow from C-H bond at that carbon back into ring to reform aromatic $\pi$ system, expelling $\text{H}^+$. Product is 4-ethylbenzoic acid plus $\text{H}^+$.

hints: Pair the $\text{H}^+$ released in the last step with the $\text{FeBr}_4^-$ made in the first step to reform the catalyst.
walkthrough:
Close the catalytic cycle**
$\text{FeBr}_3$ is a catalyst, so it must be remade. The $\text{H}^+$ lost from the intermediate reacts with $\text{FeBr}_4^-$ to give hydrogen bromide and free $\text{FeBr}_3$: $$\text{H}^+ + \text{FeBr}_4^- \rightarrow \text{HBr} + \text{FeBr}_3$$ This explains why only a small amount of $\text{FeBr}_3$ is needed.
